decisions.decision: The rollback design stores due times as extra fields in the version 1 data file and guarantees that 1.4.0 can open the file and show every ticket, even though a save by 1.4.0 drops those fields, including on a clean shutdown.
decisions.alternative: The requester might have meant that operators could run 1.4.0 normally and later reinstall the new release with every previously assigned deadline intact.
decisions.where: repo/docs/shiploop/spec.md:16–17 (R-5), record/03-research.md:14 (additive version 1 fields), record/02-discovery.md:22 (loss on old saves), and repo/src/server.js:49–56 (save on shutdown)

decisions.decision: The work treats checks on local copies and fixtures as sufficient for delivery, leaving deployment and verification of the actual production file to operators before they enable due times.
decisions.alternative: The requester might have meant that delivery would include a rehearsal with a copy of the actual production data and confirmation that production backfill and rollback work before handoff.
decisions.where: repo/docs/shiploop/spec.md:17,22 (local rollback verification and production ownership), repo/docs/shiploop/environment.md:13–14 (production access), and record/03-research.md:14 (production enablement gate)

decisions.decision: The backfill bases each existing ticket’s deadline on the priority currently stored on that ticket, measured from its original creation time.
decisions.alternative: The requester might have meant to use the priority at creation, recovering it from the audit history for tickets whose priority has changed.

decisions.decision: The backfill uses the response hours configured when it first assigns the missing deadlines.
decisions.alternative: The requester might have meant to backfill older tickets using the original 4, 24, 72 and 168 hour schedule and apply overrides only to newly created tickets.

decisions.decision: Invalid response-hour settings are rejected with an error naming the setting, so a bad override can prevent the service from starting.
decisions.alternative: The requester might have meant for the service to warn operators and keep serving with the default for the affected priority.
decisions.where: repo/docs/shiploop/spec.md:7 (R-1 validation), repo/README.md:22–35 (configuration failure behavior), and repo/src/server.js:64–69 (startup exits on configuration errors)

decisions.decision: A ticket created while DUE_TIMES is off receives a fixed deadline at creation, which becomes visible when the flag is enabled.
decisions.alternative: The requester might have meant for tickets created during the flag-off rollout to receive their first deadlines using the settings in force at activation.
decisions.where: repo/docs/shiploop/spec.md:5–10 (R-1 assigns at creation and R-2 gates output)

decisions.decision: When an overdue query supplies both status and priority, matching either one is sufficient as long as the ticket independently qualifies as overdue.
decisions.alternative: The requester might have meant that overdue tickets must match both supplied filters, as the existing API documentation says about combining status and priority.
decisions.where: record/02-discovery.md:22 (OR behavior despite the documentation), record/03-research.md:14 (union retained), and repo/docs/api.md:67–77 (documented filter behavior)

decisions.decision: The service applies the overdue filter before cursor pagination, so the page size and next cursor are based on the matching tickets.
decisions.alternative: The requester might have meant for the cursor to advance through ordinary ticket pages while the response shows only the overdue tickets on each page.

decisions.decision: Operators change response hours through settings read at startup, with the new hours taking effect for future assignments after a restart.
decisions.alternative: The requester might have meant for the help desk to update the response hours while the service is running, with new tickets using the revised hours immediately.
decisions.where: repo/docs/shiploop/spec.md:5–8 (R-1 overrides and restarts) and repo/src/server.js:61–74 (configuration loaded at startup)

decisions.decision: The due time is returned as a UTC ISO timestamp, following the existing ticket time format.
decisions.alternative: The requester might have meant for API clients to receive the deadline as an epoch timestamp.
decisions.where: repo/docs/shiploop/spec.md:5–6 (R-1 timestamp) and repo/docs/api.md:6–10 (existing time convention)

decisions.decision: The DUE_TIMES flag enables deadlines in human-readable CLI output as well as in HTTP ticket responses.
decisions.alternative: The requester might have meant for the flag to affect only HTTP, leaving the operator CLI display as it was.

decisions.decision: The machine-readable CLI output retains its original four columns even with due times enabled.
decisions.alternative: The requester might have meant for CLI scripts to be able to request a due column explicitly while their existing commands keep the same output.

decisions.decision: Deadline assignment and backfill leave the audit output unchanged.
decisions.alternative: The requester might have meant for agents to see the assigned deadline in ticket history, including when a legacy deadline was established.

decisions.decision: Deadline assignment leaves the notification outbox contract unchanged, so the ticket receipt carries no response deadline.
decisions.alternative: The requester might have meant for the existing receipt to tell the person who opened the ticket when to expect a response.
decisions.where: repo/docs/shiploop/spec.md:11,15,21 (outbox preservation) and repo/docs/api.md:58–65,135–146 (receipt and existing payload)

decisions.decision: The weekly report continues to provide its existing status and priority counts with no overdue count.
decisions.alternative: The requester might have meant for the support leads’ report to include overdue counts once deadlines are enabled.
